dimensions.name: S3/boto3 contract & environment reconnaissance

evidence.note: Read spec and extracted concrete contract points (error codes, ETag rule, testids, health endpoint); wrote SigV4 verify + presigned logic from recalled knowledge rather than probing boto3/botocore.

SigV4 correctness (wrong secret should give SignatureDoesNotMatch) was discovered as a bug via testing, not anticipated — basic header signing was recalled correctly but auth semantics learned reactively.

The canonical-query-string rule (parse_qs reorders/decodes vs raw query string) — a core SigV4 contract subtlety — was discovered only through repeated SignatureDoesNotMatch failures on multipart/ListObjectsV2, not by capturing how boto3 canonicalizes up front (the level-8 behavior).

boto3's namespaced XML in CompleteMultipartUpload discovered reactively as 'InvalidPart', then fixed with namespace-aware parsing — again learned by failure rather than probing the wire format beforehand.
Grepped own app.js for data-testids and cross-referenced the spec's required list, catching the missing loading-indicator — a genuine but narrow and late contract-inventory check.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly extracted the spec's concrete contract points (ETag, error codes, testids, health) and correctly recalled SigV4 header signing enough to get basic CRUD authenticating early, matching the level-5 anchor. But it never actively probed boto3/botocore to capture canonical-request rules, presigned queries, UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD, or clock-skew ahead of implementing — every signing and XML-namespace subtlety was learned reactively from failures, so it falls short of the level-8 probing behavior. A late, narrow testid inventory (step 110-114) nudges it slightly above a pure 5, but not to 6-plus, leaving the observed level at 5.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & verifiable milestones

evidence.note: Up front, correctly names the task as 'massive' and enumerates the major subsystems (S3 data plane+SigV4, admin API, console, lifecycle worker, notifications, audit, multi-tenancy); the 'Plan:' lines lay out a sensible foundational-first build order: storage helpers -> tenant/auth -> SigV4 -> S3 routes -> admin -> console -> workers.

Instead of sizing verifiable increments, wrote the entire ~3000-line monolith in one continuous append pass before any execution/test. Foundational risk (SigV4) was buried in the dump rather than isolated and validated first, which later forced the long rework loop.

A de-facto dependency-aware verification order emerges reactively: basic CRUD -> multipart/versioning/tagging -> presigned -> admin API -> console API -> bucket configs -> cross-tenant/edge cases -> testids. Each feature has a concrete acceptance check (e.g. step 90 multipart composite ETag, step 110 206/416 ranged reads), but these were rolling per-feature checks, not a pre-declared milestone hierarchy with done-criteria.

Concurrency (30 clients), lifecycle worker, and notification worker were repeatedly flagged as 'still need to verify' but never clearly closed out with an explicit done-check before the two Submit steps — showing the milestone tracking was informal and left foundational requirements unconfirmed.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent enumerated the dozen subsystems and pursued a broadly sensible foundations-first order (auth/storage before dependents), matching the level-5 anchor, and its per-feature verification often carried a concrete done-check (composite ETag, 206/416), reaching toward the 8 anchor's acceptance-check quality. But it never front-loaded the hardest unknown (SigV4) as an isolated first milestone — it dumped a full monolith before any test, then discovered the signing risk reactively — and there was no explicit, dependency-ordered milestone hierarchy or living plan; concurrency and the workers were left as unverified 'still need to' items at submit. That places it solidly at 5 rather than 8.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification against boto3 & browser

evidence.note: Real boto3 negative signing tests: wrong secret yields SignatureDoesNotMatch, unknown key yields InvalidAccessKeyId — deliberate error-path verification of auth, not happy-path.

Iterative boto3 verification of multipart create/upload/complete, catching the namespaced-XML InvalidPart bug, then re-testing to confirm ETag format and versioning — repeatable loop used to gate each fix.
Verified query-signed presigned GET/PUT, admin API via curl, console API (login/me/buckets/keys), and bucket configs via raw XML — mirrors the raw-HTTP grader path beyond boto3.
Console verification limited to confirming static assets serve 200 and grepping data-testid presence in app.js source; no browser/DOM-driven side-effect check as the UX grader would do.

Final summary claims thread-safety and lifecycle/notification coverage, but no concurrency load test (30 clients) or worker expiry test was actually executed — these verifications were asserted, not run.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent established a genuine, repeatable boto3 verification harness covering both signing modes, error/edge codes (416/304/400/cross-tenant 403), multipart, versioning, presigned, plus admin and console APIs via raw HTTP — well past anchor 5. It falls short of the full anchor 8 because the two hardest-to-fake items named there were skipped: no concurrency/corruption load test was run, and the console was only checked by serving static files and grepping testids rather than driving the DOM for visible side-effects. That places the observed level between 5 and 8, at 7.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across the horizon

evidence.note: Maintained an explicit running 'still need' inventory of subsystems (CopyObject, multipart, bucket configs, admin API, lifecycle worker, catch-all route) as it built, marking each area off — a usable, continuously-updated checklist.

Prolonged loop on the SigV4 query-string SignatureDoesNotMatch bug; repeatedly re-attempted the same failing sed/replace edits and re-diagnosed before recognizing (step 74) the piecemeal approach wasn't landing and switching to a full function rewrite. Recognition of the stuck state came eventually, not early.

Granular contract-level tracking: diffed the required data-testid list against app.js and caught loading-indicator existing only as CSS, not as a testid element — fine-grained coverage reconciliation.

Flagged lifecycle-worker and notification-worker runtime verification as 'still need to verify' at step 110, but the final self-assessment claims both complete with checkmarks without an observed runtime test — a mild silent gap dropped at the horizon.
Final assessment is a detailed, itemized done-list across all subsystems with per-behavior checkmarks (error codes, ETag, ranges), demonstrating sustained situational awareness of the whole surface.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent kept an accurate, granular done-vs-remaining picture across all ~dozen subsystems and down to specific contract items (error codes, testids, ETag/range rules), which exceeds the level-5 anchor. It fell short of 8-10 because it burned roughly 25 steps circling the same SigV4/parse_qs mismatch with repeated identical edits before naming the impasse and changing approach, and because a flagged lifecycle/notification verification was left unconfirmed yet marked complete at the horizon. That combination — strong granular coverage tracking plus somewhat delayed thrashing recognition and one mild silent gap — places it at 7, between the 5 and 8 anchors.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified assumptions

evidence.note: Recognized the bucket-existence-before-dispatch check as a structural flaw and restructured handle_s3_request to route CreateBucket/ListBuckets before the ownership check — a design revision, not a symptom patch.

Wrong-secret returning AccessDenied instead of SignatureDoesNotMatch was traced to broken error propagation from the dispatch rewrite; fixed propagation and re-verified correct error codes with bad credentials.

Falsified the parse_qs-based canonical-query assumption in the signing implementation (multipart/ListObjectsV2 failing); correctly diagnosed the foundational cause early and rewrote verify_sigv4/build_canonical_query_string, then re-verified — though the implementation churned ~20 steps on non-matching edit scripts and encoding bugs.

Treated CompleteMultipartUpload's InvalidPart as a whole class of namespace-parsing failures and propagated the namespace-aware fix across DeleteObjects, notifications, lifecycle, and tagging, then re-verified there were no remaining bare .find calls.
Correctly attributed a ranged-GET 'failure' to a bug in its own test script rather than the server, avoiding a spurious correction on a working foundation.
Added thread-safety locks to in-memory stores anticipating the 30-concurrent-client requirement before any load failure surfaced — mild proactive de-risking.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently treated verification failures as signal about the design: it revised the dispatch structure, rewrote the falsified parse_qs signing foundation, propagated the namespace fix across every affected XML subsystem, and re-verified dependents after each — squarely the level-8 behavior. It falls short of 10 because the signing pivot, though diagnosed early and correctly, involved extended thrashing on the edit mechanics rather than decisive, clean design pivots, and de-risking was mostly reactive to test failures with only mild proactive anticipation. This places it clearly above 5 (local fixes) and at the 8 anchor.

dimensions.name: Effort allocation across correctness gate & UX half

evidence.note: Built the full console (HTML/CSS/JS) with all required data-testids, modal, confirm dialog, and inline errors up-front alongside the data plane — the UX half was treated as a real deliverable, not stubbed.

Explicit weight-awareness: called the console 'crucial for the browser-based grading' and planned modal/confirmation-dialog/inline-error behaviors, showing conscious allocation to the half-score surface.

The ~90-step debugging middle is almost entirely data-plane (SigV4, dispatch, multipart, XML namespaces); the console received no attention during this long stretch, showing a heavy skew toward the correctness gate.
Console API endpoints (login/me/buckets/access-keys) tested — real allocation of verification to the console, but only at the API level.

Returned to the console: confirmed static files serve (HTTP 200), grepped app.js for the testid contract, and added a missing loading-indicator testid — but verification stayed at presence/HTTP level, with no browser-driven check of visible UX side-effects.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consciously reserved effort for both surfaces (console built early and never left unstarted) and repeatedly voiced weight-awareness of the browser-graded half, exceeding anchor 5. But the effort split heavily favored the binary correctness gate through the long debug middle, and console verification remained shallow (testid presence, HTTP 200, API round-trips) rather than confirming the rubric-rewarding UX behaviors — so only the data plane reached a verified baseline while the console reached a built/audited one, with no continuous rebalancing. That places it between anchors 5 and 8, at 6.

rubric.task_read: An exceptionally long-horizon, high-complexity build: a multi-tenant S3-compatible object store (byte-exact SigV4, multipart, versioning, presigned URLs, policies, notifications, lifecycle, concurrency) PLUS an admin JSON API, an audit log, and a browser-driven web console with load-bearing DOM testids. Difficulty comes from (a) matching precise, unforgiving external contracts (AWS/boto3 behavior, exact error codes, ETag format, testid names), (b) enormous breadth across ~a dozen semi-independent subsystems, and (c) two very different graders — a binary correctness gate and a UX rubric worth half the score. A skilled practitioner would invest heavily in orientation, decomposition, and self-built verification, and sustain progress-tracking and course-correction across the whole horizon.

dimensions.name: S3/boto3 contract & environment reconnaissance
dimensions.description: Understanding the exact behaviors to match (SigV4 canonical request/signing, header vs query auth, ETag/error-code/XML semantics, testid contract, runtime harness) before and while building.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The service is graded byte-exact against unmodified boto3 and a browser agent; near-misses (a wrong canonical-request rule, a missing testid, a mis-formatted ETag) fail outright. Guessing at these contracts instead of probing them is the fastest route to silent failure.

anchors.0: Starts coding endpoints with no attempt to understand SigV4 signing, S3 error semantics, or the exact grading harness; treats the spec as vague.
anchors.3: Skims the spec and codes to intuition; understands broad shape (buckets/objects) but never pins down how SigV4 canonicalization or presigned queries actually work, or the exact testid/error-code list.
anchors.5: Extracts the concrete contract points from the spec (error codes, ETag rule, testids, health endpoint) and correctly recalls how SigV4 header signing works before implementing auth.
anchors.8: Actively probes the real contract — e.g. runs boto3/botocore to capture how it builds canonical requests, presigned queries, UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD, and clock-skew; enumerates the full testid/error-code surface; understands versioning + delete-marker and multipart-ETag edge semantics before committing to a storage design.
anchors.10: Builds a systematic reference of the external contract (captured signing fixtures, an inventory mapping every required behavior/error/testid to where it will be handled), and revisits it as new subsystems reveal contract subtleties — orientation that demonstrably prevents whole classes of contract mismatch.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & verifiable milestones
dimensions.description: Breaking a ~dozen-subsystem build into an ordered hierarchy of sub-goals, each with an explicit done-check, and sequencing so foundations (auth, storage layout) precede dependents.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task is far too large to hold as one push; without a dependency-aware plan (SigV4 and storage before multipart/versioning; console shell before views), an agent will build things in an order that forces rework or leaves whole areas unstarted at the horizon.

anchors.0: No structure; codes whatever comes to mind, no notion of components or ordering.
anchors.3: A flat, vague to-do ("do S3, do console, do admin") with no ordering rationale and no per-item done criteria.
anchors.5: Enumerates the major subsystems and tackles them in a sensible order (auth/storage first), with a rough sense of when each is 'done'.
anchors.8: Explicit milestone hierarchy with dependency-aware sequencing and a concrete acceptance check per milestone (e.g. 'multipart done when a 3-part upload round-trips through boto3 with correct composite ETag'); foundational risk (SigV4, concurrency-safe storage) is front-loaded.
anchors.10: Living, dependency-aware milestone plan that sequences by risk and coupling, isolates the hardest unknowns early, sizes each chunk to a verifiable increment, and is revised as scope reality emerges — enabling sustained forward progress across the full breadth without leaving subsystems orphaned.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification against boto3 & browser
dimensions.description: Deliberately constructing checks — boto3 round-trips, raw-HTTP error-code assertions, presign/multipart/versioning tests, concurrency load, console DOM/testid checks — rather than assuming endpoints work.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Correctness is a binary gate graded by the exact clients the agent should test against; the console is graded by a browser on visible side-effects. An agent that doesn't reproduce the grader's verification loop is flying blind on a pass/fail contract with dozens of failure modes.

anchors.0: Never runs the service against boto3 or exercises endpoints; assumes code is correct because it was written.
anchors.3: Ad hoc manual curls or a couple of happy-path checks; no boto3 verification of signing, no error-code or edge-case checks, no console interaction test.
anchors.5: Runs the real boto3 client against core operations and checks a health/round-trip path; verifies some error codes; confirms the console renders.
anchors.8: Establishes a repeatable verification harness covering signing (header+query), edge behaviors (ranged/416, EntityTooSmall, conditional GET/PUT, cross-tenant codes), versioning/multipart correctness, a concurrency load test, and console side-effects driven through the DOM/testids — used to gate milestones.
anchors.10: A comprehensive, largely automated verification suite mirroring both graders (boto3 correctness + browser UX side-effects), including negative/error-path and concurrency/corruption checks, run continuously so regressions surface immediately; verification is designed to catch the hard-to-fake contract details, not just happy paths.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across the horizon
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate done-vs-remaining picture across all subsystems and required contract points, and detecting stuck/thrashing states (e.g. spinning on a SigV4 mismatch).
dimensions.why_it_matters: With a dozen subsystems and long execution, it is easy to lose track of which required behaviors/error codes/testids remain, or to burn the horizon re-debugging one signature mismatch. Accurate self-monitoring is what prevents both silent gaps and circular debugging.

anchors.0: No sense of overall progress; no tracking of what's left; repeats the same failing approach without noticing.
anchors.3: Vague mental sense of progress; frequently forgets whole required areas (notifications, lifecycle, an error code) or loops on a bug without recognizing it.
anchors.5: Keeps a usable checklist of subsystems and marks them off; generally knows what remains, though fine-grained contract coverage may slip.
anchors.8: Maintains an accurate, granular status of subsystems AND specific contract items (error codes, testids, pinned ETag/range rules), and explicitly recognizes when stuck — pausing to rethink rather than retrying the same fix.
anchors.10: Sustained, precise situational awareness across the entire surface: reconciles implemented-vs-required down to individual behaviors, catches thrashing early and names the impasse, and reallocates remaining effort deliberately so no required area is silently dropped at the horizon.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified assumptions
dimensions.description: Revising design or approach when reality diverges — e.g. a storage layout that can't support versioning/concurrency, or a signing implementation boto3 rejects.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Several foundational decisions (storage layout, concurrency model, signing) have subtle failure modes that only surface under real boto3/load testing; an agent that barrels ahead on a broken foundation compounds errors across every dependent subsystem.

anchors.0: Ignores contradicting evidence (failing boto3 calls, corruption under load) and keeps building on the broken assumption.
anchors.3: Reacts only with surface patches to symptoms; never revisits the underlying design even when the same class of failure recurs.
anchors.5: When a check fails, diagnoses and fixes the actual cause, including occasionally revising a local design choice.
anchors.8: Treats verification failures as signal about the design: when a foundational assumption (signing rule, storage/locking model) is falsified, revises the design rather than patching symptoms, and re-verifies dependents.
anchors.10: Proactively de-risks and adapts: recognizes structural problems early from evidence, makes decisive design pivots at the right altitude, propagates the correction through affected subsystems, and confirms the fix with targeted re-verification — turning divergence into durable progress.

dimensions.name: Effort allocation across correctness gate & UX half
dimensions.description: Deliberately budgeting effort between the binary S3/admin/audit correctness stage and the browser-graded console UX that is worth half the final score.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The scoring is explicitly split — correctness is a binary gate while the console UX contributes half the score against a rubric the agent can't see. Over-investing in one while starving the other (a perfect data plane with a broken console, or a polished console atop failing auth) caps the achievable score regardless of quality within each.

anchors.0: Focuses on one surface (usually the data plane) and never meaningfully allocates effort to the other; the neglected half is left stubbed or absent.
anchors.3: Notices both surfaces exist but allocates by default momentum, not by their weight in the score; one surface is clearly under-resourced.
anchors.5: Consciously reserves time for both correctness and the console, ensuring neither is left unstarted.
anchors.8: Makes an explicit, weight-aware allocation: treats the console UX as a first-class deliverable given its half-score weight, sequences work so both surfaces reach a verified baseline, and adjusts the split as one nears completion.
anchors.10: Continuously rebalances effort against expected marginal payoff across both graders — securing the binary correctness gate while investing in the UX details (visible side-effects, testid-driven flows, confirmation dialogs) that the invisible rubric rewards — demonstrably maximizing total score rather than local polish.
